source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC4203905 (BMC Med 2014;12:182, publisher's version), read in full in the built-in browser: abstract, background, methods, results and discussion (narrative review and meta-analysis), conclusions, acknowledgments (funding), competing interests, authors' contributions, reference list (refs 15, 18, 26, 33, 39, 95, 97 checked). Figures 1 and 2 checked on screen; Figure 2 was magnified in the page and its whiskers read against the gridlines. Additional file 1 (protocols, search figures, Table S1 of the seven studies, Figures S3-S4) not read.

claims.note: The second-hand figures attributed to Roerecke & Rehm 2014 match the narrative part of this paper. Former drinkers against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality: men 1.25 (1.15-1.36), women 1.54 (1.17-2.03), from 54 studies (ref 33, the authors' 2011 meta-analysis). Men drinking 60 g a day or more against lifetime abstainers: 1.00 (0.74-1.36). Ronksley's 0.75 (0.63-0.89) against current non-drinkers at 60 g or more. The 1.00 is itself second-hand here: it comes from the same authors' separate 2014 meta-analysis of chronic heavy drinking (ref 39, Open Heart), which also gives IHD incidence 1.04 (0.83-1.31). So '(Roerecke & Rehm, 2014)' should make clear which 2014 paper is meant, or say 'as cited by'. The paper's own view is that the J-shape against lifetime abstainers is clear and that Hill's criteria are fulfilled. The claim correctly presents causation as disputed. Its summary of the 2012 review (all estimates at 1-2 drinks a day significant, 0.69-0.81) uses the all-studies estimates, and Figure 1 plots those, not the stratified ones in which men's mortality at about 1-2 drinks was not significant. The claim uses both, as it should.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Lifetime abstainers and former drinkers, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Most IHD studies used current abstainers as reference. Citing the authors' 2011 meta-analysis of 54 studies (ref 33), former drinkers' IHD mortality against lifetime abstainers was 1.54 (95% CI 1.17-2.03) in women and 1.25 (1.15-1.36) in men; the definition of lifetime abstainer did not change this. Non-drinkers may be heterogeneous beyond the lifetime/former split.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Ronksley et al.: at 60 g a day or more against current non-drinkers, IHD incidence 0.76 (0.52-1.09) and IHD mortality 0.75 (0.63-0.89). The authors' chronic-heavy-drinking meta-analysis (ref 39): men drinking 60 g a day or more against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality 1.00 (0.74-1.36), mortality and morbidity combined 1.04 (0.83-1.31). Too few studies in women.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Average alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (read on screen)
anchors.extracted: Summary of the 2012 review: against lifetime abstainers, every pooled estimate at one to two drinks a day was significant (0.69 to 0.81), with women showing stronger associations and an earlier upturn. These are the 2012 all-studies estimates. Figure 1 (men's IHD mortality against lifetime abstainers) plots drinkers' points of about 0.90, 0.81, 0.74 and 0.74 at low to moderate intake, about 1.00 at the heaviest, and former drinkers at about 1.25. The 2012 stratified results for men's mortality (0.89, 0.86, not significant) are not mentioned.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions; Conclusions, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: The authors call the relationship against lifetime abstainers clearly J-shaped, say Hill's criteria are all fulfilled, and judge the evidence for a beneficial effect of low intake without heavy episodes strong. They also say uptake of drinking should not be considered a prevention option and that no amount of consumption is safe. These are interpretations; the narrative review has no stated appraisal method.

claims.overstatement: 'Set the ADH1B result aside' is slightly stronger than the source. The authors say the variant also lowers binge drinking and that the result is therefore difficult to compare with the epidemiological literature. In the same paragraph they also say Mendelian randomization may become a very useful tool. 'Questioned the comparability of' would be closer.
claims.note: Only the last clause of the statement cites this source, and it is supported in substance. The authors summarize Holmes et al. as finding higher IHD risk with higher intake at every level, that is, no protection. They note that the conclusion requires the variant to act entirely through average intake, and that the A-allele was also linked to less binge drinking.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Holmes et al. (ADH1B rs1229984): higher average consumption went with higher IHD risk at every level, that is, no protective effect. The design assumes random allocation of the allele and that its effect runs only through average intake. The A-allele was also linked to less binge drinking. Because average intake and pattern interact, the authors find the result hard to compare with the observational literature, though Mendelian randomization may become useful.

claims.note: Every number from this source matches. Seven studies; under 30 g a day; against lifetime abstainers with former drinkers not included; 0.64 (0.53-0.71) as printed; 1.12 (0.91-1.37); ratio 1.75 (1.36-2.25); I2 10% and 0%; Egger P = 0.35 and 0.58; all adjusted for age and smoking (five also for education or socio-economic status, four each for BMI and marital status). The second-hand 1.45 (1.24-1.70) comes from the 2010 meta-analysis (ref 26) of episodic heavy against moderate regular drinkers among current drinkers below 60 g a day. 'Deaths and new cases combined' matches the paper's own term 'IHD incidence', which it uses for mortality and morbidity together. The main text gives no definition of a heavy drinking occasion, no list of the seven studies, and no participant or event numbers (all in Additional file 1, not read). The first author alone searched and extracted, with eligible full texts discussed by both. No risk-of-bias tool was used. The criteria admit case-control and historical cohort designs; which designs the seven are is not stated. Recomputed: 1.12/0.64 = 1.75. The geometric midpoint of 0.53-0.71 is 0.61, and the printed interval sits 0.189 below and 0.104 above 0.64 on the log scale, so it does not fit its point estimate. The printed ratio interval 1.36-2.25 is exactly what the two printed intervals give if the pooled estimates are treated as independent (1.361-2.250). They are not independent: both come from the same seven studies, with shared lifetime-abstainer reference groups. Figure 2, read on screen at 8x against its gridlines, plots the non-heavy group at 0.64 with whiskers at about 0.50 and 0.78, and the heavy group's whiskers at 0.91 and 1.37 (as printed). So the figure matches neither printed limit for the non-heavy group. An interval of 0.53 to about 0.77 would be log-symmetric about 0.64, which suggests the printed upper limit is the misprint. The article cannot settle this. The claim's 'one figure is probably misprinted' is correct.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: Seven studies (listed only in Additional file 1, Table S1) with average intake under 30 g a day. Against lifetime abstainers, former drinkers not included, IHD 'incidence' (mortality and morbidity combined): without heavy drinking occasions RR 0.64 (95% CI 0.53-0.71), I2 10%, Egger P = 0.35; with heavy drinking occasions 1.12 (0.91-1.37), I2 0%, Egger P = 0.58. No influential study. All adjusted for age and smoking; five for education or SES; four for BMI and marital status.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Meta-analysis on drinking pattern among moderate alcohol drinkers, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: RR with against without heavy drinking occasions 1.75 (1.36-2.25), higher than the 2010 estimate; the method for this ratio and its interval is not described. The authors say the non-heavy estimate is lower than earlier average-intake analyses that ignored heavy occasions (refs 15 and 18: Roerecke & Rehm 2012; Ronksley 2011).

anchors.locator: Figure 2 (read on screen, magnified, against gridlines) and its legend
anchors.extracted: At 15 g a day: non-heavy drinkers plotted at 0.64 with whiskers at about 0.50 and 0.78; episodic heavy drinkers at 1.12 with whiskers at 0.91 and 1.37. Annotation 1.45 (1.24-1.70) from the 2010 review. The plotted non-heavy interval does not match the printed 0.53-0.71.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Drinking pattern, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors' 2010 meta-analysis (ref 26), among current drinkers who were not chronic heavy drinkers (average 60 g a day or more excluded): episodic heavy drinkers against moderate regular drinkers RR 1.45 (1.24-1.70).

anchors.locator: Methods › Searches, 1st paragraph; Methods › Meta-analysis › Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Searches from 1980 to the second week of August 2014, letters, editorials, conference abstracts, reviews and comments excluded; details in Additional file 1. Inclusion: adults 18 or over; IHD as a separate outcome (ICD-9 410-414, ICD-10 I20-25); case-control, prospective or historical cohort design; reference period over 2 weeks; a group of current drinkers averaging under 30 g a day that excluded or included episodic heavy drinking; a risk against lifetime abstainers; English, German or Spanish. Self-reported IHD and samples with IHD-related conditions excluded. No definition of a heavy drinking occasion is given in the main text.

anchors.locator: Methods › Meta-analysis › Data abstraction, 1st paragraph; Methods › Meta-analysis › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Most-adjusted RRs, lifetime-abstainer comparisons preferred. The first author did the search and abstraction; eligible full texts were discussed by both authors to consensus; primary authors were not contacted. RRs re-calculated within studies by the Hamling method; DerSimonian-Laird random effects; Q, I2, Egger, leave-one-out. No risk-of-bias assessment described.

anchors.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The ADH1B A-allele studied by Holmes et al. was linked to less binge drinking as well as lower average intake. The authors argue this makes the genetic result hard to compare with studies that separate average intake from drinking pattern.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. Addition: Figure 2 can be read. Magnified in the page and read against its gridlines, it plots the non-heavy group at 0.64 with whiskers at about 0.50 and 0.78. The heavy group is at 1.12 with whiskers at 0.91 and 1.37, matching the printed interval.

Confirmed. Addition (editors' calculation): the printed interval 1.36-2.25 is reproduced exactly (1.361-2.250) by combining the two printed intervals as if the pooled estimates were independent. They share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within the same seven studies, so they are not independent.
Confirmed. Attribution detail: the text cites the figures to ref 39 (Open Heart 2014), 'see also' ref 42 (Int J Epidemiol 2014, mortality in people treated for alcohol use disorder).
Confirmed. Figure 1 plots the men's points at about 0.90, 0.81, 0.74 and 0.74, which are the 2012 all-studies estimates, plus former drinkers at about 1.25.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed. Recomputed: geometric midpoint 0.613; log distances 0.189 below and 0.104 above 0.64; 0.64 squared / 0.53 = 0.773. Figure 2 can now be added to the evidence: it plots this interval as about 0.50 to 0.78, matching neither printed limit. 0.53 with an upper limit near 0.77-0.78 would be log-symmetric about 0.64, which points to the upper limit as the misprint, though the article cannot settle it.

Confirmed. The printed ratio interval equals the independence-based combination of the two printed intervals (1.361-2.250, recomputed). If that is how it was obtained, the correlation was not allowed for.
Confirmed: ref 33 is printed as Am J Epidemiol 2011;73:245-258; ref 36 (Kwo et al.) as Gastroenterology 2012;115 with a 1998 DOI (s0016-5085(98)70035-6).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 on the systematic part, critically low. Items 4, 7 and 9 fail on the article's own text: languages limited without reason and publication types excluded; no excluded-study list; no risk-of-bias method. Item 13 'no' is a close call, as the card says. Items 5 and 6 'no' are right (the first author searched and extracted). The narrative-part checklist in the reasoning is a fair description.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The abstract's 'strong' evidence and the Hill's-criteria conclusion rest on a seven-study pool with no risk-of-bias appraisal and on short-term surrogate-marker trials. The 2012 review is represented by its all-studies estimates, both in the text and in Figure 1. On point (4): the authors do discount the genetic result, though in the same paragraph they call Mendelian randomization potentially very useful.

missed: Figure 2 values (see key finding 1 and reporting issue 0). The non-heavy whiskers are plotted at about 0.50 and 0.78, against 0.53-0.71 in the text and abstract. This strengthens the misprint finding: the figure and the text disagree.

The printed ratio interval (1.36-2.25) can be reproduced exactly from the printed group intervals under an independence assumption (see key finding 3). This suggests both that the printed 0.53-0.71 was the input and that the shared reference groups were ignored.
